questions.q: Regarding biochemical markers to identify malnutrition, the book states:
opts: No single reliable biochemical marker exists
Serum albumin is the single reliable marker
Serum transferrin is the single reliable marker
CRP is the single reliable marker
questions.exp: Indicators: No single reliable biochemical marker to identify malnutrition. (Book p28)

questions.q: Low albumin is an indicator of:
questions.exp: Low albumin: Indicator of poor outcome. (Book p28)

questions.q: Which is a better marker than albumin for nutritional assessment?
questions.exp: S. pre albumin: Better marker. (Book p28)

questions.q: Significant weight loss is defined as unintentional weight loss of:
questions.exp: Significant weight loss: Unintentional weight loss >10% of weight in 6 months. (Book p28)

questions.q: Significant weight loss is an indicator of:
questions.exp: Significant weight loss: Indicator of poor prognosis. (Book p28)

questions.q: Which BMI value indicates poor outcome?
questions.exp: BMI <15: Poor outcome. (Book p28)

questions.q: Skin fold thickness is an indicator of:
questions.exp: Skin fold thickness: Indicator of body fat. (Book p28)

questions.q: Mid arm circumference is used as an indicator of:
questions.exp: Mid arm circumference: Muscle mass. (Book p28)

questions.q: The malnutrition universal screening tool combines BMI score, unintentional weight loss and:
questions.exp: MUST: BMI score + Unintentional weight loss + Acute disease affect score. (Book p28)

questions.q: The three components of the malnutrition universal screening tool together give the:
questions.exp: BMI score + unintentional weight loss + acute disease affect score -> Overall risk of malnutrition. (Book p28)

questions.q: The resting energy expenditure (REE) multiplier for a normal sedentary life is:
questions.exp: REE table: Normal (Sedentary life) = 1. (Book p28)

questions.q: Calorie requirement for a normal sedentary person is:
questions.exp: REE table: Normal (Sedentary life): 20 Kcal/kg/day. (Book p28)

questions.q: The REE multiplier for mild/moderate sepsis is:
questions.exp: REE table: Mild/moderate sepsis = 1.4. (Book p28)

questions.q: The REE multiplier for severe sepsis is:
questions.exp: REE table: Severe sepsis = 1.8. (Book p28)

questions.q: Severe burns have an REE multiplier and calorie requirement of:
questions.exp: REE table: Severe burns = 2, 40 Kcal/kg/day. (Book p28)

questions.q: Between enteral and parenteral nutrition, the preferred route is:
questions.exp: Enteral (Oral) > Parenteral (I/V). (Book p28)

questions.q: Advantages of enteral nutrition include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Enteral: 1. Physiological. 2. Cheap. 3. Maintains enterohepatic circulation. 4. Prevents translocation of gut bacteria. (Book p28)

questions.q: Enteral feeding prevents:
questions.exp: Enteral nutrition prevents translocation of gut bacteria. (Book p28)

questions.q: Parenteral nutrition is given by the I/V route and leads to:
questions.exp: Parenteral: I/V : Stasis. (Book p28)

questions.q: The best route of enteral nutrition is:
questions.exp: Enteral nutrition: Best route: Oral. (Book p29)

questions.q: When oral nutrition is not possible, the next deciding factor is:
questions.exp: Oral nutrition not possible -> decide by Duration of requirement. (Book p29)

questions.q: Enteral feeding needed for <3 weeks with good gastric emptying is best given by:
questions.exp: <3 weeks + gastric emptying good -> Nasogastric tube, Ryles tube. (Book p29)

questions.q: Enteral feeding needed for <3 weeks with poor gastric emptying (nausea, vomiting) is given by:
questions.exp: <3 weeks + gastric emptying poor (nausea, vomiting) -> Nasojejunal tube. (Book p29)

questions.q: Enteral feeding needed for >3 weeks with good gastric emptying is given by:
questions.exp: >3 weeks + gastric emptying good -> Feeding gastrostomy. (Book p29)

questions.q: Enteral feeding needed for >3 weeks with poor gastric emptying is given by:
questions.exp: >3 weeks + gastric emptying poor -> Feeding jejunostomy. (Book p29)

questions.q: Best position for Ryles tube insertion is:
questions.exp: Ryles tube: Best position: Sitting with neck slightly flexed. (Book p29)

questions.q: Assessment of Ryles tube placement includes:
questions.exp: Assessment of placement: Aspiration of gastric contents. (Book p29)

questions.q: Pushing air through the Ryles tube while auscultating confirms placement over the:
questions.exp: Push air -> Auscultate in epigastrium. (Book p29)

questions.q: The length of a Ryles tube is measured from the nose to the ear and then to the:
questions.exp: Ryles tube measurement: Nose - Ear - Xiphisternum. (Book p29)

questions.q: A nasojejunal tube is inserted into the jejunum under:
questions.exp: Nasojejunal tube: Inserted into jejunum under fluoroscopic guidance. (Book p29)

questions.q: The nasojejunal tube has the advantage that it:
questions.exp: Nasojejunal tube: Bypasses stomach. (Book p29)

questions.q: Feeding gastrostomy can be performed by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Feeding gastrostomy: Stamm, Witzel, PEG/RIG. (Book p29)

questions.q: Feeding jejunostomy is performed by which techniques?
questions.exp: Feeding jejunostomy: Stamm, Witzel. (Book p29)

questions.q: Compared with jejunostomy, gastrostomy feeding is:
opts: More physiological but with increased risk of aspiration
questions.exp: Gastrostomy: more physiological; ↑ risk of aspiration. (Book p30)

questions.q: The main disadvantage of gastrostomy feeding compared to jejunostomy is:
questions.exp: Gastrostomy: ↑ risk of aspiration. (Book p30)

questions.q: Stamm gastrostomy/jejunostomy is associated with:
questions.exp: Stamm: Peridrain leakage. (Book p30)

questions.q: Witzel gastrostomy/jejunostomy is associated with:
questions.exp: Witzel: Less peridrain leakage. (Book p30)

questions.q: In Stamm technique, the tube used and the suture material are:
opts: Red Robinson tube and non-absorbable suture
questions.exp: Stamm: Red Robinson tube, Non-absorbable suture. (Book p30)

questions.q: The steps of Stamm technique are:
opts: 1. Stab incision, 2. Tunnel over distal jejunum
questions.exp: Stamm: 1. Stab incision; 2. Purse string suture (small bowel). (Book p30)

questions.q: In Witzel technique the tube is buried in a tunnel made in the:
questions.exp: Witzel: Tunnel in distal jejunum. (Book p30)

questions.q: In PEG technique, step A is:
opts: Endoscope is advanced transorally into the stomach with insufflation
questions.exp: PEG step A: Endoscope is advanced transorally into the stomach with insufflation. (Book p31)

questions.q: Steps B and C of PEG technique are:
opts: Transillumination and finger indentation of the anterior abdominal wall
questions.exp: PEG steps B, C: Transillumination and finger indentation of the anterior abdominal wall. (Book p31)

questions.q: Steps D to G of PEG technique represent:
opts: Transgastric suture fixation of stomach to the abdominal wall
questions.exp: PEG steps D-G: Transgastric suture fixation of stomach to the abdominal wall. (Book p31)

questions.q: Steps H to K of PEG technique use which method to create the gastrostomy?
questions.exp: PEG steps H-K: Seldinger technique used to create a gastrostomy. (Book p31)

questions.q: Radiologically inserted gastrostomy (RIG) is indicated in:
opts: Patients where endoscopy is not possible
questions.exp: RIG indications: Patients where endoscopy is not possible. (Book p31)

questions.q: Which respiratory situation favours RIG over PEG?
questions.exp: RIG indications: Compromised respiratory function. (Book p31)

questions.q: Compromised oropharyngeal anatomy is an indication for:
questions.exp: RIG indications: Compromised oropharyngeal anatomy. (Book p31)

questions.q: Enteral feeding rate is started gradually at:
questions.exp: Rate of feeding: Started gradually: 10-20 mL/hr. (Book p31)

questions.q: If tolerated, the enteral feeding rate is increased up to:
questions.exp: Increased upto 75 mL/hr, if tolerated. (Book p31)

questions.q: Before a subsequent enteral meal one should aspirate; the next feed is withheld if the aspirate is:
questions.exp: Aspirate before subsequent meal: If aspirate is >75-100 cc: withhold next feed. (Book p31)

questions.q: Withholding the feed for a large gastric aspirate avoids aspiration due to:
questions.exp: Withhold next feed (To avoid aspiration d/t over distention of stomach). (Book p31)

questions.q: A hyperosmolar feed causes diarrhoea because of:

questions.q: Overfeeding during enteral nutrition causes:

questions.q: Parenteral nutrition is indicated in prolonged paralytic ileus lasting more than:

questions.q: A non-contracting bowel causes no transit of food leading to:

questions.q: High output faecal fistula requiring parenteral nutrition is defined as output greater than:

questions.q: Parenteral nutrition is indicated in which phase of acute severe pancreatitis?
questions.exp: Initial phase of acute severe pancreatitis. (Book p32)

questions.q: The best route of total parenteral nutrition is:

questions.q: PICC stands for:

questions.q: Risk of pneumothorax is least with which central line?

questions.q: The amount of TPN solution given is:

units.title: Nutritional Assessment: Indicators
units.guide: No single biochemical marker identifies malnutrition: low albumin foretells poor outcome while pre albumin tracks better, >10% unintentional weight loss in 6 months and BMI <15 signal poor prognosis, and skin fold thickness reads body fat while mid arm circumference reads muscle mass.

units.title: MUST Tool & Energy Requirement
units.guide: The MUST tool adds BMI score, unintentional weight loss and acute disease affect score into an overall malnutrition risk, while the REE table climbs from 1 (20 Kcal/kg/day sedentary) through 1.4 and 1.8 sepsis to 2 with 40 Kcal/kg/day in severe burns.

units.title: Enteral vs Parenteral & Route Algorithm
units.guide: Enteral beats parenteral because it is physiological, cheap, maintains enterohepatic circulation and blocks bacterial translocation. When oral fails, duration and gastric emptying decide: under 3 weeks a nasogastric or nasojejunal tube, beyond 3 weeks a gastrostomy or jejunostomy.

units.title: Ryles & Nasojejunal Tubes
units.guide: Insert the Ryles tube sitting with the neck slightly flexed, measure nose-ear-xiphisternum, and confirm by aspirating gastric contents or auscultating pushed air over the epigastrium; the nasojejunal tube goes in under fluoroscopy and bypasses the stomach.

units.title: Invasive Feeding Tubes: Stamm, Witzel, Gastrostomy vs Jejunostomy
units.guide: Gastrostomy (Stamm, Witzel, PEG/RIG) is more physiological than jejunostomy (Stamm, Witzel) but risks aspiration. Stamm uses a Red Robinson tube through a stab incision and purse string with peridrain leakage; Witzel tunnels the distal jejunum and leaks less.

units.title: Technique of PEG & RIG
units.guide: PEG runs from transoral endoscope insufflation through transillumination and finger indentation, transgastric suture fixation and a Seldinger gastrostomy; RIG steps in when endoscopy is impossible or respiratory or oropharyngeal function is compromised.

units.title: Enteral Principle & Complications
units.guide: Start feeds at 10-20 mL/hr and climb to 75 mL/hr if tolerated, withholding the next feed when aspirates exceed 75-100 cc. Tube problems (blockage, migration, leakage) are the m/c complication, while osmotic diarrhoea from hyperosmolar feeds leads feeding-regime trouble.

units.title: Parenteral Nutrition: Indications & Routes
units.guide: TPN serves paralytic ileus beyond 72 hours, non-contracting bowel, short bowel syndrome, >500 cc faecal fistulas, acute IBD needing bowel rest and early severe pancreatitis. The central line is the best route, PICC sits in between, and peripheral lines are least preferred for thrombophlebitis.

units.title: Central Line: Vein Comparison & Assessment
units.guide: Subclavian lines thrombose and infect least but pneumothorax most and dominate TPN; the internal jugular is easiest to place and the commonest vein overall; femoral lines infect most. The tip must sit in the SVC just above the right atrium, and the X-ray also rules out pneumothorax.

units.title: PICC Line
units.guide: Ultrasound-guided into a peripheral vessel with the tip just above the right atrium, a PICC lasts 2-3 months for chemotherapy, TPN or prolonged antibiotics - but demands regular dressing and care.

units.title: TPN Solution & Types
units.guide: 1-2 litres over 24 hours in a 20:30:50 protein:fat:carbohydrate mix, as 3-in-1 or 2-in-1 bags with trace elements and vitamins but no fibre. High osmolar bags raise CO2 and thrombosis risk, low osmolar bags suit pulmonary failure, and low volume low protein bags suit renal failure.

units.title: Monitoring on Nutritional Support
units.guide: Daily: pulse, BP, temperature, weight and abdominal gain (>1 Kg/day is the earliest sign of overfeeding), input-output charts and food consumed. Plasma: Na, K, urea, creatinine, glucose, magnesium, phosphate and LFTs, weekly once the regime is stable.

units.title: Complications of TPN
units.guide: Catheter related sepsis is the m/c line complication, confirmed by matching peripheral and central cultures, endoluminal brush or tip culture; lines also bring pneumothorax, arrhythmias, thrombosis, air embolism and migration. The regime brings hyperglycemia, cholestasis (withhold TPN), zinc deficiency, refeeding and electrolyte imbalance, and 25% of long-term users derange liver enzymes - managed with lipid free solutions.

units.title: Refeeding Syndrome
units.guide: Feeding a chronically starved patient flips catabolism into an insulin-driven anabolic state that drags phosphate, magnesium, potassium and calcium into cells; hypophosphatemia drives the derangement and CHF/arrhythmia kill. Risk: BMI <16, >15% weight loss in 3-6 months, >10 days without intake, low pre-feeding electrolytes - prevent with slow feeds (max 10 Kcal/kg/day to full needs over 4-7 days), electrolyte monitoring and thiamine.

units.title: Post Operative Fluid Requirement
units.guide: Goal directed replacement: insensible losses 30-40 mL/kg/day, Ryles aspirate with NS + KCl, drains with RL and urine with NS/DNS.

units.title: K+, Daily Electrolytes, Fluids & Calories
units.guide: Potassium waits until day 2 because surgical cell injury dumps K+ out of cells; daily needs run Na 50-90, K 50, Ca 5, Mg 1 mmol. Hartmann's (Na 131, K 5, Ca 2, Cl 111, lactate 29) contrasts with normal saline (154/154), colloids expand blood volume, and calories come 4-4-9 from carbohydrate, amino acid and fat.
